strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: this appears to be the first publicly available, successful application of the prior-data fitted network (PFN) framework to graph-structured data, combining a tabular foundation model backbone (LimiX) with attention-based message-passing adapters.

The graph prior is thoughtfully designed (multi-level stochastic block models combined with a modified Barabási–Albert process, plus graph-aware structural causal models for attribute generation) and grounded in observed properties of real graphs (community structure, core-periphery structure). The two-stage generation process is clearly explained and computationally efficient.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: 13 datasets spanning node classification and regression, homophilous and heterophilous graphs, tabular and text-based features, with comparisons against strong, well-tuned GNN baselines (with modern architectural improvements) and the strongest existing GFMs (G2T-FM variants), in both ICL and finetuning regimes, with 10 repetitions and standard deviations.

The paper includes a useful control experiment (Table 4): finetuning LimiX with randomly initialized graph adapters performs substantially worse than finetuned GraphPFN, supporting the claim that synthetic pretraining (not just the architecture) drives the gains.

The limitations section (Appendix A) is honest and specific, covering scalability constraints (OOM results are visible in the main tables), prior-data mismatch (acknowledged and analyzed, e.g., density mismatch with hm-prices, topology mismatch with city-roads-M), limited ablations, inherited LimiX restrictions, and restriction to node-level tasks.
The authors transparently note that benchmark evaluations during pretraining were used only for post-hoc analysis, not model selection or early stopping.
weaknesses: Scalability limitations are significant: the model requires processing the whole graph in memory, leading to OOM failures on several benchmark datasets (city-reviews, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, pubmed), and the SOTA claim is restricted to datasets with up to 50,000 nodes. This narrows the practical reach of a 'foundation model'.

Ablations are limited, as the authors themselves acknowledge. In particular, the contribution of the masked graph modeling loss, the value of the multi-SBM + preferential-attachment design versus simpler priors (e.g., a single SBM), and the effect of the MLP/GNN mixture probability in attribute generation are not empirically validated. The prior's realism is supported only qualitatively via visualizations in Appendix C, not by quantitative comparisons of structural statistics with real graphs.

ICL performance is mixed: while competitive on some datasets, GraphPFN (ICL) underperforms substantially on others (e.g., avazu-ctr 21.67 vs 32.39 for G2T-LimiX; questions 12.30 vs 20.19 for finetuned G2T-LimiX), and the headline claim rests primarily on finetuned results rather than the in-context capability that motivates the PFN framework.

Several methodological details that affect reproducibility and fairness of comparison are deferred or sparse: the finetuning protocol (which components are finetuned, hyperparameter budgets relative to baselines), exact adapter configurations, and how the 'RL data split' differs from standard splits are not fully specified in the main text.

The claim of being 'the first publicly available successful implementation of PFN framework for graph data' is difficult to verify and should be softened or supported with a more thorough survey of prior graph-PFN attempts.

The 10%/10%/80% train/val/test split favors the few-shot regime where PFN-style methods shine; results under more label-rich regimes, where GNNs and LightGBM-NFA are typically stronger, are not reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question: whether the PFN recipe (synthetic-prior pretraining + in-context learning) can be successfully transferred to graph data, going beyond the hand-crafted-feature approach of G2T-FM and TabGFM.

The graph prior is thoughtfully designed and well-motivated: the combination of multiple degree-corrected SBMs, a modified Barabási–Albert process for core–periphery structure, and graph-aware structured causal models (mixed MLP/GNN neurons, optional LapPE) is a sensible and efficient recipe for producing diverse synthetic attributed graphs.

The architecture modification is clean and well-integrated: attention-based message-passing adapters grafted onto LimiX blocks preserve the tabular model's ability to handle heterogeneous features and labels while adding a local structural channel, and the design is clearly explained (Figure 1).

The evaluation protocol is reasonably rigorous: comparisons against well-tuned classic GNN baselines with modern improvements (Platonov et al. style), two G2T-FM backbones, 10 repetitions with mean and standard deviation, and both ICL and finetuning regimes.

The additional ablation in Table 4 (randomly initialized vs. pretrained graph adapters) is a valuable control that directly tests whether finetuning gains come from pretraining rather than merely from added message-passing capacity, and the result is convincing.
The limitations appendix is honest and specific (scalability, prior-coverage gaps, limited ablations, class-count restrictions, node-level-only tasks), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The central 'state-of-the-art' claim (Observation 2) is overstated given incomplete comparisons: finetuning failed with OOM on four of the benchmark datasets (city-reviews, avazu-ctr, twitch-views, pubmed in Tables 2–3), so the model is simply not evaluated against the baselines there. State-of-the-art on 'up to 50,000 nodes' is only established on the subset where the model runs.

In-context learning performance — the core selling point of the PFN framework — is mixed. GraphPFN (ICL) loses to G2T-LimiX (ICL) on most datasets (e.g., 21.67 vs 32.39 on avazu-ctr, 59.95 vs 71.08 on twitch-views, 12.30 vs 15.31 on questions, and even worse with LapPE on questions at 9.62). This suggests the designed prior transfers substantially worse than the authors' framing implies.

The authors themselves attribute failures on hm-prices and city-roads-M to prior–downstream mismatch (e.g., pretraining graphs capped at ~194K edges vs. 10.7M edges in hm-prices). This reveals a significant fragility: the approach's success appears tightly coupled to how well the hand-tuned prior happens to match the benchmark, which partially undermines the claim that 'a well-designed prior is an effective strategy' as a general recipe.

Ablations are thin relative to the design space introduced: no ablation of the masked graph modeling loss (is the 0.1-weighted MGM term actually needed?), no ablation of the multi-SBM + BA structure prior vs. simpler SBM alone, no analysis of the SCM mixing probability p, and no comparison against simply finetuning G2T-LimiX with message-passing-style features. The authors acknowledge this but it limits what can be concluded about which components matter.

The pretrained graph adapters were monitored on GraphLand test sets every 100 steps during pretraining (Section 3.2). While the authors state this was post-hoc only, evaluating four benchmark datasets (artnet-exp, tolokers-2, city-roads-M, artnet-views) throughout pretraining creates an implicit selection-pressure concern that is not fully dispelled, particularly since artnet-exp and tolokers-2 are among the strongest reported results.

Heavy dependence on the LimiX checkpoint with all layers frozen except adapters means the contribution is arguably an adapter-tuning study on top of an existing tabular foundation model rather than a graph foundation model in a strong sense; the interaction between frozen backbone capacity and graph-specific learning is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code or model release is stated, pretraining consumed ~8 A100 GPUs for 6 days, and the prior involves many hyperparameter distributions whose exact choices (number/size of blocks, degree sequences, sampling distributions) are described only qualitatively in the main text.

Scalability is a fundamental limitation for a paper claiming to build a graph foundation model: full-graph processing with OOM failures at ~150K nodes and dense graphs leaves the practical utility narrow, and the restriction to ≤10 classes further narrows applicability.

strengths: Novel and significant contribution: to the best of the reviewer's knowledge, this is the first publicly available successful implementation of the prior-data fitted network (PFN) framework for graph data, addressing a real gap in graph foundation models (GFMs) that currently rely on hand-crafted graph features bolted onto tabular foundation models.

The proposed graph prior is thoughtfully designed and well-motivated: the combination of multiple degree-corrected SBMs to produce 'rough' overlapping clusters, augmentation with a modified Barabási–Albert preferential attachment process for core-periphery structure, and graph-aware structured causal models (mixed MLP/GNN neurons, optional LapPE) for attribute generation is a principled and computationally efficient way to generate diverse synthetic attributed graphs. The visualizations in Appendix C support the realism claims.

The architecture is sensible and well-integrated: message-passing adapters layered onto the LimiX backbone preserve the PFN in-context learning machinery while adding a local graph-attention channel; initializing from a pretrained tabular foundation model and freezing non-adapter layers is computationally pragmatic.

Strong empirical results with careful evaluation: experiments follow the established G2T-FM protocol, cover 13 diverse datasets (classification and regression, homophilous and heterophilous, tabular and text-based features), use 10 runs with mean and standard deviation, and include extensively tuned strong GNN baselines with modern architectural improvements. Finetuned GraphPFN achieves the best results on 7 out of 10 finetunable datasets, sometimes by large margins (e.g., artnet-exp, hm-prices, artnet-views).

The additional experiment in Appendix B (finetuning LimiX with randomly initialized graph adapters) is a valuable ablation that isolates the contribution of graph-prior pretraining from the mere presence of graph adapters, showing large performance drops without pretraining (e.g., 46.19 vs 60.77 on tolokers-2).

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Appendix A) covering scalability, prior-domain mismatch, limited ablations due to compute, inherited backbone constraints, and restriction to node-level tasks. The authors also correctly emphasize that benchmark evaluations during pretraining were used only post-hoc, not for model selection.
weaknesses: In-context learning performance is mixed: GraphPFN (ICL) is clearly worse than G2T-LimiX (ICL) on several datasets (e.g., hm-prices 68.02 vs 74.96, city-roads-M 58.93 vs 64.53, avazu-ctr 21.67 vs 32.39, twitch-views 59.95 vs 71.08), and notably even underperforms LightGBM-NFA on twitch-views. The headline ICL claim is therefore weaker than the finetuning claim, and the prior-mismatch explanation is plausible but not experimentally validated.

Scalability is a substantial limitation: the model OOMs on 4 of 13 datasets during finetuning, restricting the evaluation to graphs of at most ~50k nodes. The restriction to at most 10 classes further narrows the scope. While honestly discussed, this limits the 'foundation model' framing, which typically implies broad applicability.

Ablations are admittedly limited: the importance of the masked graph modeling objective, the specific prior components (multi-SBM vs. BA augmentation, LapPE injection, mixing probability p), and the finetuning protocol are not systematically studied. Given the central claim that 'a well-designed prior' is the key to success, ablations of the prior components would substantially strengthen the paper.

The architectural contribution itself is relatively incremental (graph-masked attention adapters added to an existing tabular backbone); much of the novelty resides in the prior design, which makes the missing prior ablations more consequential.

Some evaluation details raise minor fairness/reproducibility questions: PCA to 64 dimensions is applied only to certain datasets for GraphPFN finetuning (Appendix D) without clarity on whether baselines received the same treatment; the optional LapPE variant of GraphPFN performs inconsistently (sometimes harmful, e.g., questions ICL 9.62), and selection between GraphPFN variants is not fully specified.
Pretraining cost is significant (8 A100 GPUs for ~6 days, 4M synthetic datasets), and no inference-time cost comparison with G2T-FM or GNN baselines is provided, which matters for practical adoption.

strengths: Novel and timely contribution: GraphPFN is, to the authors' knowledge, the first publicly available PFN pretrained specifically on graph data for node-level tasks, going beyond prior work (G2T-FM, TAG, TabPFN-GN) that merely tabularizes graphs with hand-crafted features and applies unmodified tabular foundation models.

The synthetic graph prior is thoughtfully designed and well motivated: multi-level stochastic block models combined with preferential attachment to capture community plus core-periphery structure, and graph-aware structured causal models (MLP/GNN mixed neurons, optional LapPE) that tie attributes to structure. The ablation in Appendix B.3 against Erdős–Rényi, degree-corrected SBM, and preferential attachment alternatives shows the complex prior yields better downstream performance in most cases, empirically supporting the design.

Evaluation is broad and careful: 13 diverse datasets (classification/regression, homophilous/heterophilous, tabular and text-based features), strong baseline suite (tuned classic GNNs with modern tricks, LightGBM+NFA, prior GFMs, and the strongest PFN-based GFMs G2T-FM and TAG), both ICL and finetuning regimes, ensembling, 10 runs with standard deviations, and average-rank summaries. Finetuned GraphPFN achieves the best results on 10 of 13 datasets, often with substantial margins.

The control experiment in Appendix C (LimiX + randomly initialized graph adapters, finetuned identically) convincingly rules out the alternative explanation that gains come merely from the added adapter capacity rather than the synthetic pretraining.
Learning-curve monitoring during pretraining is explicitly described as post-hoc analysis only (no test-set early stopping or model selection), which is an appropriate methodological disclosure.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Appendix A): scalability/memory constraints, prior coverage limited to social/information networks, ≤10-class constraint inherited from LimiX, and restriction to node-level tasks. Code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope of evaluation is restricted to small/medium datasets (≤~170K nodes, ≤10 classes) with a 10/10/80 split; the model processes the entire graph in memory and even ran out of memory during finetuning on pubmed (requiring reporting ICL only), so claims about 'graph foundation models' rest on a fairly narrow slice of the graph-ML landscape.

The prior-alignment analysis (Tables 3–4) shows imperfect coverage: e.g., synthetic homophily has mean 0.06 while real datasets reach 0.69, assortativity and average pairwise distance distributions only partially overlap real values; the paper asserts synthetic characteristics 'cover' real ones, which is only loosely supported for some statistics.

In-context learning results are mixed rather than dominant: on classic datasets GraphPFN (ICL) loses to GAT on average rank, and to G2T-LimiX (ICL, E) on amazon-ratings and facebook; the strongest claims for the method rely on the finetuning + ensembling regime, which blurs the 'foundation model / in-context' narrative somewhat.

The architectural novelty is incremental: the core mechanism is scaled dot-product attention masked by adjacency, inserted as an adapter into LimiX blocks; the main contribution is the prior and the pretraining recipe rather than a new architecture.

Some supporting analyses are under-powered: the prior ablation (Table 5) uses only pretraining Stage 1, is evaluated on a single checkpoint with no variance estimates, and the adapter ablation (Table 6) covers only the GraphLand subset; a few dataset-specific preprocessing inconsistencies (PCA to 64 on some text datasets but not pubmed) complicate interpretation.

The ensembling protocol differs subtly across methods (e.g., TAG's inherent ensembling vs. 10-seed averaging for GraphPFN/G2T-FM; feature shuffling excluded for G2T-FM because it hurt performance), so head-to-head rank comparisons between (ICL, E) methods involve slightly non-identical procedures.

strengths: Novel and well-executed direction: GraphPFN is, to the authors' knowledge, the first PFN-based graph foundation model that is actually pretrained on synthetic attributed graphs, going beyond prior TFM-based approaches (G2T-FM, TAG, TabPFN-GN) that only augment hand-crafted graph features for a tabular model.

The graph prior is thoughtfully designed and justified: multi-level degree-corrected SBMs combined with preferential attachment target observed properties of real graphs (irregular community structure, core-periphery structure), and the SCM-based attribute generation with mixed MLP/GNN neurons is a clean way to inject structure-dependence into features and targets.

Empirical evidence for the central claims is convincing: extensive comparison against strong baselines (well-tuned classic GNNs with modern tricks, G2T-FM, TAG, prior GFMs), 10 repetitions with mean/std, results on both the GraphLand benchmark and classic datasets, covering classification and regression, homophilous and heterophilous graphs.

Important ablations are provided: (i) pretraining on simpler random graph models (Erdős–Rényi, SBM, PA) shows the complex prior matters in most cases (Table 5); (ii) random graph adapters vs. pretrained adapters (Table 6) shows finetuning gains come from pretraining, not just the extra capacity; (iii) numerical alignment of real vs. synthetic graph characteristics (Tables 3-4).

Learning-curve analysis during pretraining (Figure 2) with an explicit statement that test data was not used for model selection, and a thorough, honest limitations section covering scalability, prior coverage, class-count limits, and restriction to node-level tasks.
weaknesses: Scope is restricted to small/medium-scale datasets (≤~170K nodes) and ≤10 classes; ICL requires processing the entire graph at once, so the applicability of a 'foundation model' framing is limited, and the authors' own limitations acknowledge this is unresolved.

The ICL claim is weaker than the finetuning claim: on several datasets GraphPFN (ICL) underperforms G2T-LimiX (e.g., avazu-ctr 30.41 vs 32.39, tolokers-2 60.33 vs 61.45), and wins on classic datasets largely only against weak prior GFMs; G2T-LimiX and TAG-LimiX remain very competitive, so the incremental benefit of graph-specific pretraining in the ICL regime is moderate on average rank rather than dramatic.

There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the masked graph modeling (MGM) loss or of the random-feature input augmentation, both of which are nontrivial design choices affecting reported numbers; the ensembling comparison also mixes regimes, which complicates reading the tables even though regimes are labeled.

The heavy reliance on the LimiX checkpoint makes it hard to fully disentangle how much of the strength is inherited from the tabular backbone versus learned from the graph prior; the random-adapter ablation partially addresses this but is run only on the GraphLand datasets.
The prior is tuned toward social/information networks; performance is worse on road networks (city-roads-M) even in the ablation, and the paper offers only a hypothesis for this mismatch.

Practical evaluation gaps: GraphPFN ran out of memory when finetuning on pubmed (ICL reported instead), and PCA preprocessing was applied to two datasets, introducing mild inconsistencies in the experimental protocol.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: GraphPFN is, to the authors' knowledge, the first publicly available PFN pretrained specifically on graph data for node-level tasks, a meaningful step beyond G2T-FM/TAG, which only tabularize graphs via hand-crafted features without graph pretraining.

The proposed graph prior is a thoughtful and novel combination (multi-level degree-corrected SBMs + preferential attachment for core-periphery structure, plus graph-aware structured causal models with mixed MLP/GNN neurons and optional LapPE for attribute generation), and it is supported by substantive analysis: visual inspection (App. B.1), quantitative alignment with real-world graph statistics (Tables 3-4), and a genuine ablation against simpler random graph models (Table 5) showing the prior matters.

Comprehensive and fairly tuned evaluation: strong GNN baselines with Platonov-style improvements and hyperparameter tuning, LightGBM+NFA, multiple prior GFMs, and the strongest PFN-based GFMs (G2T-FM, TAG), across two dataset collections covering classification/regression, homophilic/heterophilic graphs, and tabular/text features, with 10 repetitions and mean/std reported.

Results are strong in both regimes: competitive-to-leading ICL performance (best average rank on GraphLand) and state-of-the-art after finetuning on 10 of 13 datasets, often with substantial margins (e.g., twitch-views, hm-prices).

Good ablation of the pretraining claim (Table 6): finetuning LimiX with randomly initialized but architecturally identical graph adapters degrades performance substantially, supporting that synthetic-graph pretraining rather than adapter capacity alone drives the gains.

Honest, detailed limitations section (Appendix A) covering scalability, prior domain coverage, inherited LimiX constraints, and restriction to node-level tasks; reproducibility is aided by released code and detailed training/ensembling protocols (App. D).
weaknesses: Scope of evaluation is limited to small/medium graphs (up to ~168K nodes) and at most 10 classes; the paper does not demonstrate the promise of a 'graph foundation model' at scales where foundation models typically matter, and the ablation study (Table 5) only covers stage-1 pretraining, which weakens the evidence for the prior's value at full scale.

Statistical support for some claims is thin: on classic datasets, GraphPFN (FT, E) loses to G2T-LimiX (FT, E) on amazon-ratings (45.89 vs 46.05) and mean differences on several datasets are comparable to or smaller than reported standard deviations; '10 out of 13' headline relies partly on close margins, and pubmed FT results are missing due to OOM, so average-rank comparisons on classic datasets are computed over somewhat different method subsets.

Potential prior-realism mismatch is underexplored: Table 4 shows median homophily of 0.0 and median clustering/distance values that are extreme relative to some real datasets (e.g., city-roads-M's avg. pairwise distance of 129.89), and the acknowledged failure of the prior to match road networks (Table 5, city-roads-M) suggests transfer risk on structurally dissimilar domains.

The learning-curve analysis (Figure 2) repeatedly evaluated test performance during pretraining; although the authors state it was post-hoc only, this is a methodological gray area that is asserted rather than independently verifiable.

Several gains conflate multiple techniques (random feature augmentation, 10-seed ensembling, finetuning recipes borrowed from Rubachev et al.); while baselines are compared in matched regimes, a cleaner isolation of GraphPFN's specific contributions (e.g., adapters alone vs. adapters + augmentation) would strengthen the causal story.

The architecture is essentially LimiX plus 1-hop masked attention adapters, and pretraining freezes the backbone; the contribution is more a careful system/prior design than an architectural or theoretical advance, which limits how broadly the findings generalize beyond the chosen backbone.
